The Federal Forage Fee Act of 1993 establishes a methodology for determining fees for grazing livestock on federal lands. Congress asserts that public lands provide essential conservation and economic benefits and that fees for their use should be equitable and represent fair market value.

The Act requires that all grazing operations on federal land adhere to existing environmental and land-use regulations, including the Clean Air Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act.

The bill defines a complex formula for calculating the annual Federal Forage Fee, based on:
*   The weighted average private land lease rate (WAPLLR) for sixteen Western states.
*   The private lease forage value ratio (PLFVR).
*   Adjustments for the "nonfee cost differential" (reflecting the costs of grazing on public versus private land).
*   A "net production differential" comparing cash receipts from federal versus non-federal livestock production.

The Secretaries of Agriculture and the Interior must calculate the fee annually. To ensure market stability, annual fee adjustments are capped, preventing the new rate from exceeding 125% or falling below 75% of the previous year’s fee.
ref:
Federal Forage Fee Act of 1993 - Subjects grazing operations on Federal land to applicable Federal, State, and local environmental and land use requirements. 
Sets forth a forage fee formula for lands under the jurisdiction of the Department of Agriculture and the Department of the Interior.

The Merchant Marine of World War II Congressional Gold Medal Act authorizes the presentation of a Congressional Gold Medal to the United States Merchant Marine in recognition of their dedicated and vital service during World War II. 

The bill acknowledges the Merchant Marine’s indispensable role in transporting military personnel, equipment, and supplies across all theaters of operation, noting that they endured a higher per capita casualty rate than any other branch of the military. 

Following the award, the gold medal will be housed at the American Merchant Marine Museum for display and research. The Secretary of the Treasury is authorized to strike and sell bronze duplicates of the medal to cover production costs. Under this legislation, the gold medal is designated as a national medal, and all medals produced under the Act are considered numismatic items.

Merchant Marine of World War II Congressional Gold Medal Act (Sec. 3) This bill requires the Speaker of the House of Representatives and the President pro tempore of the Senate to arrange for the award, on behalf of Congress, of a single gold medal to the U.S. Merchant Marine of World War II, in recognition of their dedicated and vital service during World War II.  Following its award the medal shall be given to the American Merchant Marine Museum where it will be available for display and research.

The Fair Access to Investment Research Act of 2016 directs the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to revise its regulations to provide a "safe harbor" for investment fund research reports. 

Under the Act, a research report regarding a "covered investment fund" published by a broker or dealer will not be considered an illegal offer for sale of a security, even if the broker or dealer is participating in the fund's registered offering. The legislation requires the SEC to update regulation 230.139 to ensure that such research is not restricted by conflicts of interest regarding active offerings. 

The Act specifically prevents self-regulatory organizations from prohibiting members from publishing research simply because they are also participating in the fund's offering. Furthermore, it exempts these reports from certain filing requirements under the Investment Company Act of 1940. The bill includes an interim rule allowing for this safe harbor if the SEC fails to adopt the required revisions within 180 days. Importantly, the Act does not limit the application of existing antifraud or antimanipulation provisions of federal securities laws.
ref: Fair Access to Investment Research Act of 2016 This bill directs the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to revise a specified regulation to create a safe harbor for certain publications or distributions of research reports by brokers or dealers distributing securities. The revised regulation shall declare that a published or distributed investment fund research report shall not be deemed to constitute an offer for sale or an offer to sell a security that is the subject of the offering pursuant to an effective registration statement, even if the broker or dealer is participating or will participate in the registered offering of the covered investment fund's securities. The covered investment fund research report shall indeed be deemed to satisfy the regulation's requirements as well as those of any self-regulatory organization. The SEC shall not impose specified conditions and requirements when implementing the safe harbor.  Until the SEC has adopted such safe harbor revisions, and the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) has revised a related rule, a covered investment fund shall be deemed to be a security listed on a national securities exchange that is not subject to a certain filing requirement of the Investment Company Act of 1940.

The Prescription Drug Monitoring Act of 2016 mandates that states receiving federal funding for Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs (PDMPs) implement specific operational requirements within two years of enactment. 

Covered states must require practitioners to consult their PDMP before prescribing Schedule II, III, or IV controlled substances and periodically thereafter. Programs must provide proactive notifications to practitioners regarding potential substance misuse and require dispensers to report controlled substance transactions within 24 hours. States are also required to publish quarterly de-identified data sets and annual reports. Failure to comply may result in the withholding of federal grant funds.

Additionally, the Act requires states to participate in an interstate data-sharing hub. The Attorney General and the Secretary of Health and Human Services will award a grant to establish this hub, which must allow for fee-free access by authorized users, maintain state ownership of data, and adhere to industry exchange standards. The bill authorizes $2 million in appropriations for fiscal years 2017 through 2020 to facilitate the development and maintenance of this data-sharing infrastructure.
ref: Prescription Drug Monitoring Act of 2016 This bill requires a state that receives grant funds under the prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP) or the controlled substance monitoring program to comply with specified requirements. The Department of Justice (DOJ) or Department of Health and Human Services may withhold grant funds from a state that fails to comply.  Additionally, the bill requires a state to share its PDMP data with other states through a data-sharing hub established by DOJ.

The Promoting Financial Literacy and Economic Opportunity Act of 2015 amends the Internal Revenue Code to establish a tax credit for for-profit organizations that fund economic and financial literacy programs for students. 

The credit is equal to 50 percent of the costs incurred by an eligible organization to implement a "qualified program" as defined by the Elementary and Secondary Education Act. Under this program, 25 percent of the expenditures must be for direct activities, while 75 percent must be used for subgrants.

The Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Secretary of Education, is limited to awarding this credit to no more than 20 organizations per taxable year. A majority of these recipients must be socially or economically disadvantaged small businesses, women-owned businesses, veteran-owned businesses, or entities with assets not exceeding $60 billion. Priority is given to programs serving urban or rural underserved areas. Organizations may elect not to claim the credit, and the credit amount reduces any other allowable deductions for the same expenses. The legislation takes effect for taxable years beginning after its enactment.
ref: Promoting Financial Literacy and Economic Opportunity Act of 2015 This bill amends the Internal Revenue Code to allow up to 20 for-profit organizations in any taxable year a business-related tax credit for 50% of the amount paid or incurred to carry out activities to improve the quality of student understanding of personal finance and economics. The Department of the Treasury shall determine which for-profit organizations are eligible for the credit, ensuring that a majority of credit recipients are: (1) either a socially and economically disadvantaged small business concern, a small business concern owned and controlled by women, or a small business concern that is at least 51% owned by veterans, or (2) do not have more than $60 billion in assets. In determining the eligibility of a for-profit organization, Treasury shall give priority to organizations that have programs serving either urban or rural underserved areas.

The Outer Continental Shelf Revenue Sharing Act of 2005 amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to modify revenue-sharing provisions and establish procedures for offshore energy leasing.

The bill mandates that the Secretary of the Interior delineate lateral boundaries between coastal states for federal jurisdictional areas, consistent with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. 

It imposes a moratorium until June 30, 2012, on leasing activities in specified "affected areas" (including regions off the coasts of California, Oregon, Washington, the Atlantic, and parts of the Gulf of Mexico), while exempting existing marine sanctuaries. After the Secretary establishes state boundaries, the Governor of a state—with legislative consent—may petition for a resource assessment of an affected area. If the assessment is approved, the state may petition the Secretary to open areas located more than 20 miles from the coastline for oil, gas, or renewable energy leasing. 

States where production begins under this process are entitled to a share of qualified revenues, provided at least 25% of those funds are allocated to specific environmental or coastal conservation purposes. The Secretary is directed to establish regulations for gas-only leases.
ref:
Outer Continental Shelf Revenue Sharing Act of 2005 - Amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (OCSLA) regarding the coastal impact assistance program to: (1) repeal references to leasing moratoria; (2) redefine a "producing state" as one that begins production on a leased tract on or after the date of enactment of this Act, regardless of whether the leased tract was on any date subject to a leasing moratorium; (3) repeal the exclusion of certain revenues from "qualified Outer Continental Shelf revenues;" and (4) repeal the exclusion of certain leased tracts from the statutory formula for payments to coastal political subdivisions.

Directs the Secretary of the Interior to delineate the lateral boundaries between coastal states in areas of the Outer Continental Shelf under exclusive federal jurisdiction.

Prescribes guidelines for petitions to lease within the seaward lateral boundaries of coastal states.

Includes guidelines under which a state shall share in qualified Outer Continental Shelf revenues as of the date production begins under this Act.

Directs the Secretary of the Interior to issue implementing regulations, including procedures for entering into gas-only leases.

The Developmental Disabilities Assistance and Bill of Rights Act Amendments of 1993 updates the federal framework for supporting individuals with developmental disabilities. The Act establishes a formal policy stating that disability is a natural part of the human experience and that individuals with developmental disabilities are entitled to self-determination, independence, and full inclusion in society.

The bill defines the purpose of federal assistance as ensuring access to culturally competent services, specifically by supporting State Developmental Disabilities Councils, protection and advocacy systems, university-affiliated programs, and national initiatives. The legislation emphasizes that individuals and their families should be the primary decision-makers regarding their care.

Additionally, the Act introduces technical and administrative requirements, such as mandating public notice and comment for federal onsite reviews of state advocacy systems. It also adjusts funding authorizations, setting specific spending levels for fiscal year 1994 and providing for such sums as necessary for fiscal years 1995 and 1996 across the various grant programs established under the Act.
ref:
Developmental Disabilities Assistance and Bill of Rights Act Amendments of 1993 - Amends the Developmental Disabilities Assistance and Bill of Rights Act to revise the Act's statements of findings and purpose and to declare related policy. 
Requires:  (1) advance public notice of any Federal programmatic and administrative review; (2) solicitation of public comment on State systems to protect and advocate the rights of persons with developmental disabilities; (3) inclusion of the comment findings in the onsite visit report; and (4) distribution of the review results. 
Removes from the definition of "State," as it applies to university affiliated programs under the Act, references to the Northern Mariana Islands, American Samoa, and the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. 
Authorizes appropriations under the Act for priority area activities, protection and advocacy of the rights of individuals with developmental disabilities, university affiliated programs, and projects of national significance.

This bill amends Section 496 of the Higher Education Act of 1965 to strengthen due process protections and increase transparency for institutions of higher education during the accreditation process.

The legislation mandates that accrediting agencies provide institutions with clear notice of deficiencies, reasonable time to correct them, and the right to a hearing before adverse actions are finalized. It establishes a formal appeals process through an independent, jointly appointed arbitration panel, outlines rules for legal representation, and dictates how appeal costs are allocated.

Additionally, the bill imposes new constraints on accrediting agencies regarding institutions under interim state-appointed management, ensuring accreditation is not terminated solely due to such management without documented evidence of other deficiencies. 

Finally, the bill requires that all meetings—including hearings, deliberations, and votes regarding accreditation standards or specific institutional status—be open to the public. Agencies must post agendas at least seven days in advance. The Secretary of Education is tasked with implementing these requirements, with the stipulation that they cannot reduce existing due process protections for accredited institutions.
ref:
Amends the Higher Education Act of 1965 to revise due process standards governing the accreditation process of educational institutions.

 Requires accrediting agencies and associations to provide educational institutions with: (1) written notice of deficiencies and a reasonable time period to correct such deficiencies; (2) advance notice of any adverse action and an opportunity for a hearing; and (3) a right to appeal an adverse action to an independent and impartial arbitration panel.

Requires accrediting agencies and associations to: (1) ensure consistent application of accreditation standards to an educational institution's governing board in receivership; and (2) allow public access to meetings involving accreditation recommendations.

Authorizes the Secretary of Education to issue regulations to further define due process requirements for the accreditation process.

Matsunaga Hydrogen Research, Development, and Demonstration Act of 1990 to revitalize federal hydrogen energy initiatives. ref: Robert S. Walker and George E. Brown, Jr. Hydrogen Energy Act of 2001 - Amends the Spark M. The Health Care Fraud Prevention and Paperwork Reduction Act of 2000 establishes the Commission on Billing Codes and Forms Simplification to standardize health care billing forms and reduce billing codes.

To improve Medicare administration, the bill mandates a process for physicians to request written clarification on billing codes from carriers, providing immunity from future audits for following such guidance (excluding fraud). It also requires the restoration of a toll-free physician hotline.

New evaluation and management (E&M) guidelines cannot be implemented by the Health Care Financing Administration (HCFA) without physician assessment, formal goal-setting, and at least four regional pilot projects. 

The bill introduces protections regarding Medicare overpayments, including:
*   Requirements for individualized notice of billing problems during audits.
*   A three-month interest-free repayment window for overpayments.
*   Prohibitions on using extrapolated penalties for first-time errors.
*   Limits on reimbursement delays following audits.

Finally, the Act restricts the conduct of federal inspectors during investigations, prohibiting the carry of deadly weapons into private physician offices and requiring valid arrest warrants except in cases of flight or identified danger.
ref:
Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to establish a process under which a physician may request, in writing from a carrier, assistance in addressing questionable codes and procedures under the medicare program.
Sets forth provisions concerning: (1) policy development regarding evaluation and management guidelines; and (2) medicare overpayments.

The "No Second Chances for Murderers, Rapists, or Child Molesters Act of 1998" expresses the sense of Congress that individuals convicted of murder should receive the death penalty or life imprisonment without parole, and those convicted of rape or dangerous sexual offenses against children under 14 should receive mandatory life imprisonment without parole.

The bill directs the U.S. Sentencing Commission to amend federal sentencing guidelines to reflect these mandates. To combat recidivism, the Act penalizes states that release offenders who later commit similar violent crimes in other jurisdictions. If an offender with a prior conviction for murder, rape, or a dangerous sexual offense commits a subsequent crime of that nature, the Attorney General is authorized to redirect federal law enforcement assistance funds from the state(s) of the prior conviction. These funds are to be transferred to the victims (or their estates) of the subsequent offense and used to cover the costs of the offender’s apprehension, prosecution, and incarceration in the state where the new crime occurred. Finally, the Act requires the Attorney General to collect and distribute data regarding recidivism rates for these specific violent crimes.
ref:
No Second Chances for Murderers, Rapists, or Child Molesters Act of 1998 - Expresses the sense of the Congress that any individual convicted of:  (1) murder should receive the death penalty or be imprisoned for life without the possibility of parole; and (2) rape or a dangerous sexual offense involving a child under age 14 should be imprisoned for life without the possibility of parole. 
Requires the Attorney General to transfer the following amounts from Federal law enforcement assistance funds for a State that convicted a person of a first offense of murder, rape, or a dangerous sexual offense to a State that convicts that person for a subsequent such offense:  (1) up to $100,000 for transfer to each victim of the subsequent offense; and (2) the cost of incarceration, prosecution, and apprehension of such person.  Sets forth provisions regarding situations where a person has a prior conviction in more than one State. 
Requires the United States Sentencing Commission to amend the Federal sentencing guidelines to provide that whoever is guilty of: (1) murder shall be punished by death or by life imprisonment; and (2) rape or a dangerous sexual offense shall be punished by life imprisonment. 
Directs the Attorney General to collect and distribute data to the President, Members of Congress, State governments, and officials of localities and penal and other institutions participating in the Uniform Crime Reports program which includes:  (1) the number of murders, rapes, and dangerous sexual offenses committed by persons previously convicted of one of these offenses; and (2) the percentage of cases in which a person convicted of murder, rape, or a dangerous sexual offense in one State commits a second offense in another State.

The Contributions Legally Interdicted from Noncitizens To Our Nonprofits Act of 2016 (CLINTON Act) amends the Internal Revenue Code to restrict charitable organizations established or managed by certain federal officials from accepting contributions from individuals or entities connected to foreign governments.

Under the bill, any 501(c)(3) organization controlled or managed by current or former federal officials—including the President, Vice President, Members of Congress, Senate-confirmed appointees, and federal judges—would lose its tax-exempt status if it knowingly solicits or accepts contributions from foreign government agencies, international organizations, their employees, or members of royal families.

The bill imposes a tax equal to the value of any prohibited contribution accepted. If an organization discovers it has accepted such a contribution, it must return the funds within 30 days to avoid violating the prohibition. The restrictions apply to those who have held relevant federal offices within the 20-year period preceding a contribution, and to those connected to foreign governments at any time within the 20-year period preceding the contribution.
ref: Contributions Legally Interdicted from Noncitizens To Our Nonprofits Act of 2016 or the CLINTON Act of 2016  This bill amends the Internal Revenue Code to prohibit a federal official organization from being treated as a tax-exempt organization under section 501(c)(3) for any period after the date on which the organization knowingly or willingly accepts or solicits any contribution from any person connected to a foreign government.  A tax-exempt organization is a "federal official organization" if one or more current or former specified federal officials established, control, or actively participate in the management of the organization.  If the organization accepts a contribution from any person and learns that that the person is connected to a foreign government after the acceptance, it will not be treated as knowingly or willingly accepting the contribution if the contribution is returned within 30 days of learning of the status of the person.  The bill imposes a tax on any federal official organization that knowingly or willingly accepts any contribution from any person connected to any foreign government in an amount equal to the amount of the contribution.

The Reduce Expenditures in Nuclear Infrastructure Now (REIN-IN) Act proposes significant reductions in United States nuclear forces and related infrastructure spending, citing the end of the Cold War, fiscal concerns, and the adequacy of existing force levels. 

The bill mandates several funding prohibitions, including:
*   Stopping development or procurement of new long-range penetrating bombers, new intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), and the F-35’s nuclear capabilities.
*   Terminating specific projects, including the W78 life extension program, the Mixed Oxide Fuel Fabrication Facility, the Chemistry and Metallurgy Research Building replacement, the Uranium Processing Facility, and the Medium Extended Air Defense System.
*   Capping submarine-launched ballistic missiles at 250 and restricting deployed ballistic-missile submarines to no more than eight.
*   Limiting high-alert ICBMs to 150.
*   Conditioning B61 life extension funding on meeting a $5 billion cost cap.

The legislation also requires the Secretaries of Defense and Energy to report annually on implementation progress and mandates that the President provide a comprehensive annual accounting of expenditures for all nuclear weapons and programs.
ref: Reduce Expenditures in Nuclear Infrastructure Now Act or the REIN-IN Act - Prohibits the obligation or expenditure of funds authorized to be appropriated to the Department of Defense (DOD) for FY2014-FY2023: (1) for the research, development, test, and evaluation (RDT&E) or procurement of a long-range penetrating bomber aircraft; (2) to procure an SSBN-X submarine (and prohibits the use of such funds for FY2024 and thereafter to procure more than eight such submarines); or (3) for the RDT&E or procurement of a new intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM). Prohibits the obligation or expenditure of funds authorized to be appropriated for FY2014 or thereafter for DOD or the Department of Energy (DOE): (1) to make the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter aircraft capable of carrying nuclear weapons; (2) until the Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of Energy jointly certify that the total cost of the B61 life extension program has been reduced to not more than $5 billion; (3) for the W78 life extension program; (4) for the mixed oxide fuel fabrication facility project; (5) to replace the chemistry and metallurgy research building at Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, New Mexico; or (6) for the uranium processing facility at the Y-12 National Security Complex, Oak Ridge, Tennessee. Prohibits Navy forces, beginning in FY2020, from including more than eight operational ballistic-missile submarines available for deployment. Prohibits the use of DOD funds for FY2014 or thereafter: (1) to maintain more than 250 submarine-launched ballistic missiles; (2) to maintain more than 150 intercontiental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) on a 24-hour, high alert status; or (3) for the medium extended air defense system. Requires initial and annual reports from the Secretaries of Defense and Energy outlining their respective plans to carry out the requirements of this Act. Directs the President to submit to Congress an annual report containing a comprehensive accounting by the Director of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) of the amounts obligated or expended by the federal government for each nuclear weapon and related nuclear program during the fiscal year covered by the report for the life cycle of such weapon or program.

This bill establishes financial restrictions on House of Representatives candidates who exceed specific campaign contribution limits. 

Under the legislation, if a candidate’s total campaign funds (including existing cash and new contributions) exceed $600,000 per election cycle, or if contributions from multicandidate political committees exceed $300,000, the excess is categorized as "excess campaign contributions." 

For candidates who exceed these thresholds, the bill mandates that:
1. Excess contributions are subject to federal income tax, removing the tax-exempt status usually granted to political organizations.
2. Candidates are disqualified from receiving the "lowest unit charge" for broadcast advertising.
3. Candidates are ineligible for reduced third-class postal mailing rates.

To access reduced postage rates or lowest broadcast charges, candidates must certify they have not obtained excess contributions for the current election cycle. The bill expresses a sense of Congress that any increased costs to the U.S. Postal Service resulting from these changes should be offset by the tax revenue generated from taxing excess campaign contributions.
ref:
Amends the Internal Revenue Code with respect to political organizations to establish a campaign contribution limitation scheme applicable to the campaign committee of a candidate for election to the House of Representatives.  Provides that excess campaign contributions received by such an organization shall be included in its gross income. 
Amends the Communications Act of 1934 and Federal postal service law to condition the lowest unit charge for campaign ads upon a candidate's certification of compliance with such contribution limitation. 
Expresses the sense of the Congress that additional costs incurred by the United Postal Service in providing reduced rates of postage pursuant to this Act should be funded out of revenues attributable to this Act.

The Clinical Laboratory Compliance Improvement Act of 2004 amends the Social Security Act to enhance whistleblower protections and oversight for clinical diagnostic laboratories. 

The bill mandates that providers and laboratories post notices informing employees how to report noncompliance regarding testing, quality, or personnel training. It prohibits retaliation against employees who report violations or participate in investigations, granting them the right to seek judicial relief, including reinstatement, back pay, and attorney’s fees, within a two-year window. Adverse employment actions, such as denied promotions or negative credentialing decisions, are explicitly defined as prohibited retaliation.

Additionally, the Act requires that standard surveys of these facilities be conducted on an unannounced basis. Individuals who provide advance notice of such surveys face civil penalties of up to $2,000. The bill also establishes protocols for investigative organizations to process reports of noncompliance and requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to submit annual reports to Congress regarding these oversight activities. 

These provisions take effect on January 1, 2005.
ref:
Clinical Laboratory Compliance Improvement Act of 2004 - Amends title XVIII (Medicare) of the Social Security Act to require each provider or clinical laboratory approved for participation under Medicare to provide clinical diagnostic laboratory tests to post in a conspicuous place a notice to employees that indicates the manner in which to report instances of noncompliance with conditions of participation.

Prohibits such a provider or clinical laboratory from discriminating against or retaliating in any manner against any employee because that employee, or any other person, has presented a grievance or complaint, or has initiated or cooperated in any investigation or proceeding of any kind, relating to the clinical diagnostic laboratory tests performed or other requirements and prohibitions of Medicare. Provides for judicial action for any employee so aggrieved.

Requires the investigative organization, upon receipt of a report of an instance of noncompliance, to: (1) provide notice to the Secretary and other investigative organizations involved of receipt of the report within three business days, using a standard format and manner of transmission developed by the Secretary for such purpose; (2) promptly determine whether to investigate the report; and (3) if appropriate, promptly investigate it.

Requires that the Secretary, in measuring the performance of an investigative organization under contract, to provide for appropriate adjustments to payments for failure to carry out the responsibilities of this Act. Subjects each provider or clinical laboratory to a standard survey, including verification of compliance with requirements, conducted without prior notice. Makes liable for civil monetary penalties any individual who notifies (or causes to be notified) a provider or laboratory of the time or date on which such a survey is scheduled to be conducted.

Regarding electric output facility bonds, the bill protects existing bonds issued before the enactment of the "Comprehensive Electricity Competition Act" by ensuring they are not reclassified as "private activity bonds" due to market competition actions required by the Act, such as open-access transmission or retail competition. The United States-Afghanistan Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) Act of 2011 mandates that the President negotiate a bilateral status of forces agreement with the Government of Afghanistan within 90 days of enactment. 

The Act requires that this agreement include three specific provisions: prohibiting a permanent United States military presence or base in Afghanistan; establishing a timeline for the complete withdrawal of all U.S. Armed Forces, Department of Defense civilian employees, and contractors within one year of the agreement's signing; and confirming that any temporary U.S. military presence is at the request of the Afghan government. 

Additionally, the bill expresses the sense of Congress that such an agreement should be submitted to the Senate for ratification as a treaty or be subject to specific congressional authorization. Finally, the President is required to submit the finalized agreement, which may include a classified annex, to the relevant congressional intelligence committees for review by members of Congress.
ref:
United States-Afghanistan Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) Act of 2011 - Directs the President to seek to enter into a bilateral status of forces agreement with the government of Afghanistan which shall: (1) prohibit the permanent basing or military presence of U.S. Armed Forces in Afghanistan; (2) provide, no later than one year after the date on which such agreement is entered into, for the complete redeployment from Afghanistan of the U.S. Armed Forces and Department of Defense (DOD) civilian employees and contractors; and (3) establish that the temporary presence of U.S. Armed Forces in Afghanistan is at the request of the government of Afghanistan. Authorizes such agreement to provide for specific activities or missions of the U.S. Armed Forces in Afghanistan.

Each 12-member board consists of individuals recommended by the state’s Governor and must be chaired by a local elected official. Federal employees may not constitute a majority of the board. Members serve four-year terms, with staggered initial appointments. 

The boards are tasked with providing public input and recommendations to the Secretary regarding land use, management, and the needs of local landowners. The Secretary must consult with the board before finalizing designations and publish their recommendations. Additionally, the boards are responsible for monitoring species recovery progress and periodically reviewing the scientific data supporting habitat designations. Subject to appropriations, the Secretary may provide funding to help private-sector board members obtain technical expertise to interpret scientific data and educate the local community regarding conservation issues.
ref:
Endangered Species Community Advisory Board Act of 1995 - Amends the Endangered Species Act of 1973 to direct the Secretary of the Interior to establish an Endangered Species Community Advisory Board in connection with the designation of an area under the Act as critical habitat or as a National Wildlife Refuge. 
Allows the Secretary, subject to the availability of appropriations, to make funds available to facilitate the participation of individuals from the private sector on such Boards to ensure public input into the designation of such areas or Refuges. 
Requires the Board to:  (1)  monitor and periodically report to the Secretary on progress made in the conservation and recovery of species for which the critical habitat or Refuge was designated; and (2) periodically review and report to the Secretary regarding the continued accuracy and sufficiency of the scientific findings that were the basis of such designation.

The Freedom to Mourn in Peace Act of 2011 amends Title 38 of the United States Code to restrict public demonstrations at veteran funerals, memorial services, and bereavement ceremonies. The bill prohibits demonstrations on the property where a funeral is held unless authorized by the property owner or cemetery superintendent.

Furthermore, the Act bans demonstrations within 1,000 feet of such property if they impede access or egress. It also prohibits demonstrations within 150 feet of access routes during a window beginning 60 minutes before and ending 60 minutes after a service if the demonstration causes noise or distractions that disturb the peace of the event. These restrictions apply only when signage clearly indicates that a funeral is taking place.

The bill defines "demonstration" to include picketing, the use of sound amplification, the display of banners or placards, and the distribution of literature. The stated purpose of the legislation is to protect the families and friends of deceased veterans from emotional distress and to ensure they can mourn in peace.
ref:
Freedom to Mourn in Peace Act of 2011 - Expands the prohibition on demonstrations at certain funerals, memorial services, or bereavement ceremonies for a deceased veteran to any property where such a service is held unless the demonstration has been approved by the cemetery superintendent or the owner of the property on which the funeral is held. (Current law only prohibits such demonstrations on property of a cemetery under the control of the National Cemetery Administration or on the property of Arlington National Cemetery.)

Extends to 1,000 feet the distance within which certain demonstrations that impede access to or egress from such a cemetery or property are prohibited during the period beginning 60 minutes before and ending 60 minutes after such a service, provided that there is a visible sign at applicable distances stating the time interval during which a service will be held.

The Helping to Encourage Real Opportunities (HERO) for At-Risk Youth Act modifies and expands the Work Opportunity Tax Credit and extends the authorization for empowerment zones.

The bill expands the tax credit for youth employees by allowing year-round employment eligibility, provided the employee works no more than 20 hours per week while attending secondary school. It also establishes a new category for the tax credit: "at-risk youth." This category includes individuals aged 16–24 who have not been regularly employed or attending school for the six months prior to hiring and lack basic skills, as well as foster children aged 16–20 who were in foster care within the year prior to being hired.

Additionally, the Act extends the designation period for empowerment zones from December 31, 2016, to December 31, 2019. These changes apply to individuals hired after the date of the Act’s enactment.
ref: Helping to Encourage Real Opportunities (HERO) for At-Risk Youth Act  This bill amends the Internal Revenue Code, with respect to the work opportunity tax credit, to:    change the credit for summer youth employees to a credit for youth employees who will be employed for not more than 20 hours per week during any period between September 16 and April 30 in which the individual is regularly attending any secondary school,   increase the amount of the credit for youth employees, and   expand the credit to include at-risk youth.  An "at-risk youth" is any individual who is certified by the designated local agency as:    having attained age 16 but not age 25 on the hiring date,   having not regularly attended specified schools or been employed during the six-month period preceding the hiring date, and  not readily employable by reason of lacking a sufficient number of basic skills.   The term also includes individuals who have been certified as having attained the age of 16 but not age 21 on the hiring date and as an eligible foster child who was in foster care during the 12-month period ending on the hiring date.  The bill also extends until December 31, 2019, the designation period for certain tax-favored empowerment zones.

The PROSPERS Act (Preserve Rights Of States and Political subdivisions to Encourage Retirement Savings Act) amends the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA). The bill establishes that state-run or qualified local government payroll deduction savings programs do not constitute "employee pension benefit plans" under ERISA.

To qualify for this exemption, programs must meet specific criteria, including:
*   State or local government administration and oversight.
*   Mandatory employer participation limited to ministerial duties (e.g., payroll deductions and notice distribution).
*   Prohibition on employer contributions, monetary incentives, or discretionary authority.
*   Voluntary participation for employees, including potential automatic enrollment features.
*   Strict security and enforcement mechanisms provided by the governmental entity.

The bill also defines "qualified political subdivisions," allowing local governments to establish such programs if they meet specific population, geographic, and administrative criteria. By exempting these state-facilitated programs from ERISA’s definition of a pension plan, the legislation aims to protect such programs from federal regulatory preemption, provided they comply with the outlined structural and operational requirements.
ref: Preserve Rights Of States and Political subdivisions to Encourage Retirement Savings Act or the PROSPERS Act  This bill amends the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) to specify that states and certain political subdivisions may establish and administer voluntary payroll deduction retirement savings programs for private sector employees that are not considered employee pension benefit plans or pension plans covered by ERISA if the plans meet certain requirements.  The bill requires the plans to be established, implemented, and administered by states or political subdivisions. The plans must also be voluntary for employees and meet other specified requirements, including restrictions on the involvement of employers and obligations to enforce the rights of employees.

The Small Company Capital Formation Act of 2011 amends the Securities Act of 1933 to direct the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to create a new exemption from registration for small securities offerings. Under this provision, issuers may offer and sell up to $50 million in equity or debt securities within a 12-month period.

Key requirements for this exemption include:
* Securities must not be "restricted," allowing for public sale.
* Issuers must file annual audited financial statements and may be required to provide periodic disclosures regarding their business, financial condition, and use of funds.
* The SEC may implement "bad actor" disqualification provisions similar to those in the Dodd-Frank Act.
* Issuers are permitted to solicit interest from potential investors prior to filing an offering statement.

The Act mandates that the SEC review and adjust the $50 million offering limit every two years. Additionally, it requires the Comptroller General to conduct a study on the impact of state-level "Blue Sky" laws on Regulation A offerings and report the findings to Congress. The bill also establishes conditions under which these exempted securities are treated as "covered securities" under federal law.
ref:
Small Company Capital Formation Act of 2011 - (Sec. 2) Amends the Securities Act of 1933 (Act) to direct the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to exempt from its regulation a class of securities for which the aggregate offering amount of all securities sold within the prior 12-month period in reliance upon such exemption does not exceed $50 million. Restricts any such exemption to equity securities, debt securities, and debt securities convertible or exchangeable to equity interests, including any guarantees of such securities.

Subjects to civil liability certain violations arising from offering or selling securities by use of prospectuses and communications. Authorizes the SEC to: (1) require an issuer of such exempted class of securities to make periodic disclosures available to investors regarding the issuer, its business operations, financial condition, corporate governance principles, and use of investor funds; (2) require the issuer to file electronically with the SEC and distribute to prospective investors an offering statement which includes this information; (3) provide for the suspension and termination of this disclosure requirement with respect to that issuer; and (4) prescribe exemption disqualification requirements, substantially similar to regulations adopted in accordance with the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, under which the exemption shall not be available to the issuer and related persons, including predecessors, affiliates, officers, directors, and underwriters.

Requires the SEC to: (1) review and increase biennially such offering amount limitation, as appropriate; and (2) report to certain congressional committees its reasons for not increasing the amount if it determines not to do so.

 Exempts from state regulation the securities covered and required exempted from SEC regulation by this Act.

(Sec. 3) Directs the Comptroller General to study the impact of state laws regulating securities offerings (Blue Sky laws) on offerings made under Regulation A (which specifies the terms and conditions of exemption from the registration requirements of the Securities Act of 1933).

The bill requires applicants for voter registration—whether via motor vehicle agencies or by mail—to provide a photographic copy of documentation proving United States citizenship, based on guidelines established by the Election Assistance Commission in consultation with the Departments of Homeland Security and State. These requirements also extend to states that do not have traditional registration or that allow same-day registration.

Additionally, the Act mandates that all individuals voting in person in federal elections must present current, valid photo identification. Individuals voting by mail are required to submit a copy of a current, valid photo identification with their ballot. These provisions apply to the regularly scheduled federal general election in November 2004 and all subsequent federal elections.
ref:
Federal Election Integrity Act of 2004 - Amends the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 to require any individual who desires to register or re-register to vote in an election for Federal office to provide the appropriate State election official with proof that the individual is a U.S. citizen. Requires proof of citizenship in States without registration requirement and States permitting same day registration.

Amends the Help America Vote Act of 2002 to prohibit the appropriate State or local election official from: (1) providing a ballot for an election for Federal office to an individual who desires to vote in person unless the individual presents to the official a current and valid photo ID; or (2) accepting any ballot of an individual voting by mail without a copy of a current photo ID.

The Federal Facilities Clean Water Compliance Act of 1993 amends the Federal Water Pollution Control Act to ensure federal agencies comply with environmental regulations. The Act waives the federal government’s sovereign immunity, making federal facilities subject to all federal, state, and local water pollution requirements, including administrative orders, civil penalties, and reasonable service charges. 

While federal employees are shielded from personal civil liability for acts within the scope of their duties, they remain subject to criminal sanctions. The Act authorizes the EPA Administrator and the Secretary of the Army to issue compliance orders and assess civil penalties (up to $25,000 per day) against federal agencies for violations. It establishes a public hearing process for challenged orders and creates a special Treasury fund for collected penalties to be used for water remediation at federal sites. Additionally, the Act expands the definition of "person" to include federal agencies and clarifies the definition of "radioactive materials" regarding certain unlicensed facilities.
ref:
Federal Facilities Clean Water Compliance Act of 1993 - Amends the Federal Water Pollution Control Act to waive immunity of the United States with respect to Federal, State, interstate, and local requirements, administrative authorities, sanctions, and penalties concerning water pollution control.  Absolves Federal employees of personal liability for civil penalties under water pollution control laws for acts or omissions within the scope of official duties.  Makes Federal employees subject to criminal sanctions under Federal or State water pollution control laws, but prohibits applying criminal sanctions to Federal agencies. 
Permits the imposition of civil penalties or the issuance of compliance orders against Federal agencies determined to be in violation of specified water pollution control or permit requirements. Authorizes the suspension or revocation of permits.  Provides for the deposit of penalties into a fund to be used for water remediation and other restorative and preventive projects at Federal facilities. 
Includes Federal agencies within the definition of "person" for purposes of such Act.

The bill asserts that the Fifth Amendment's "public use" requirement for land seizures is being undermined by the inclusion of economic development as a valid justification for taking private property.

The legislation mandates that the power of eminent domain may only be exercised for "public use" and explicitly excludes economic development from that definition. This restriction applies to all exercises of eminent domain by the federal government, as well as any exercises by state or local governments that involve the use of federal funds. The bill aims to protect homeowners and small businesses from government-sanctioned property transfers to private parties, arguing that such seizures disproportionately harm marginalized populations and violate the original intent of the Constitution.
ref: Protection of Homes, Small Businesses, and Private Property Act of 2005 - Declares that the power of eminent domain shall be available only for public use, which shall not be construed to include economic development. Applies such limitation to all exercises of eminent domain by the federal government or by state and local governments through the use of federal funds.

The American Indian Equal Justice Act aims to limit sovereign immunity for Indian tribes by making them subject to judicial review in specific civil matters. The bill mandates that tribes, tribal corporations, and members collect and remit state excise, use, and sales taxes on purchases made by non-members. 

The legislation grants U.S. district courts original jurisdiction over civil claims against tribes involving federal laws, contracts, and torts. It establishes an "Indian Tort Claims Procedure," establishing that tribes are liable for negligent or wrongful acts to the same extent as private individuals or corporations, excluding punitive damages and pre-judgment interest. 

Furthermore, the bill grants federal consent for state courts to exercise jurisdiction over certain tort and contract claims against tribes, regardless of existing requirements for tribal consent. It also amends the Indian Civil Rights Act of 1968 to provide U.S. district courts jurisdiction over civil rights actions against tribes, explicitly waiving tribal immunity to the extent necessary to enforce these provisions. The Act applies to cases commenced on or after its enactment.

Permits a State to bring an action in a U.S. district court to enforce the requirement. 
Grants U.S. district courts:  (1) original jurisdiction in any civil action or claim against an Indian tribe, in matters arising under the Constitution, laws, or treaties of the United States; (2) jurisdiction of any civil action or claim against an Indian tribe for liquidated or unliquidated damages for cases not sounding in tort that involve any contract made by the governing body of the Indian tribe or on behalf of an Indian tribe; and (3) subject to Indian tribe tort claims procedure provisions under this Act, jurisdiction of civil actions in claims against an Indian tribe for money damages, accruing on or after the enactment of this Act for loss of property, personal injury, or death caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of an Indian tribe under circumstances in which the Indian tribe, if it were a private individual or corporation, would be liable to the claimant in accordance with the law of the State where the act or omission occurred. 
Sets forth Indian tort claims procedure provisions.  Excepts any case relating to a controversy about membership in an Indian tribe. 
Grants consent to institute a civil cause of action against an Indian tribe in a State court on a claim arising within the State, including a claim arising on an Indian reservation or Indian country, in any case in which the cause of action:  (1) arises under Federal or State law; and (2) relates to tort claims or claims not sounding in tort that involve any contract made by the governing body of an Indian tribe on or behalf of a tribe.  Provides, in any tort action brought in a State court against an Indian tribe, for that tribe to be liable to the same extent as a private individual or corporation under like circumstances, but not to be liable for interest prior to judgment or for punitive damages. 
Amends title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 (the Indian Civil Rights Act) to grant U.S. district courts jurisdiction in any civil rights action alleging a failure to comply with rights secured by the requirements under such title.

States that a violation of this Act shall: (1) be treated as a violation of a rule defining an unfair or deceptive act or practice of the Federal Trade Commission Act; and (2) be subject to civil and criminal penalties.

The Geriatric Care Act of 2001 aims to improve medical care for the elderly by addressing physician training and service coordination.

First, the Act amends the Social Security Act to encourage advanced training in geriatrics. It excludes up to three additional full-time equivalent residents specializing in geriatric medicine or geriatric psychiatry from the federal limitations placed on the number of residents a hospital or health center may count for direct and indirect Graduate Medical Education (GME) payments.

Second, the Act expands Medicare Part B coverage to include "care coordination and assessment services" for individuals with serious, disabling chronic conditions. These services—provided by certified care coordinators—include initial and annual health assessments, medication management, multidisciplinary care conferences, and caregiver counseling. The Act mandates that Medicare cover 100 percent of the allowable costs for these services, effectively eliminating coinsurance for patients. 

The Secretary of Health and Human Services is directed to establish necessary procedures, with the coverage provisions becoming effective on January 1, 2003.
ref: Geriatric Care Act of 2001 - Amends title XVIII (Medicare) of the Social Security Act (SSA) with respect to payments to hospitals, rural health clinics, or Federally qualified health centers for direct graduate medical education costs and the limitation on the number of full-time-equivalent residents in allopathic and osteopathic medicine. Provides for the disregard of up to three geriatric residents in applying such limitation.Amends SSA title XVIII, as amended by the Medicare, Medicaid, and SCHIP Benefits Improvement and Protection Act of 2000, to provide for Medicare coverage of care coordination and assessment services to an individual with a serious and disabling chronic condition.

The Federal Reserve Reform Act of 1995 proposes several structural and operational changes to the Federal Reserve System:

*   **Advisory Committee:** It replaces the Federal Open Market Committee with a Federal Open Market Advisory Committee, consisting of Federal Reserve bank presidents, to advise the Board on open-market operations.
*   **Consultation:** The Board must meet periodically with the Secretary of the Treasury, the Director of the OMB, and the Chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers.
*   **Leadership Terms:** It mandates that the President appoint the Federal Reserve Chair and Vice Chair, subject to Senate confirmation. The Chair’s term is linked to the President's term, while the Vice Chair serves a four-year term.
*   **Transparency:** The Board must publicly disclose any changes to intermediate monetary policy targets on the date they are adopted.
*   **Oversight:** The bill expands the Comptroller General’s authority to audit certain financial communications and requires the Board to submit its annual budget and expenditure projections to the President for transmittal to Congress.
ref:
Federal Reserve Reform Act of 1995 - Amends the Federal Reserve Act to abolish the current Federal Open Market Committee, on which the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (the Board) sits, and replace it with a Federal Open Market Advisory Committee, on which the Board does not sit, which shall advise the Board on the conduct of open-market operations. 
Requires the Board to meet and consult with the Secretary of the Treasury, the Director of the Office of Management and Budget, and the chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers during specified periods. 
Revises the term of the Chairman of the Board to expire on January 31 of the first calendar year beginning after the end of the term of the President who appointed the Chairman.  Provides for performance of the duties of Chairman and Vice Chairman in the event of absence, unavailability, or vacancy. 
Mandates that each Board-adopted change in the intermediate targets for monetary policy be disclosed to the public upon its date of adoption. 
Amends Federal law to:  (1) instruct the Comptroller General to audit written communications by members of the Board or officers or employees of the Federal Reserve System with respect to financial transactions; and (2) mandate an annual transmittal to the President and the Congress of all estimated receipts and proposed expenditures of the Board and all Federal Reserve banks for the current year and the next two succeeding years.

The Agricultural Market Promotion Program Amendments Act of 1993 modifies the existing Market Promotion Program to prioritize small and medium-sized beginning exporters. Specifically, the Act mandates that at least 30 percent of program funds be directed toward these entities during fiscal years 1994 and 1995.

The legislation introduces new requirements for branded promotion assistance, ensuring that program funds supplement, rather than replace, an entity’s existing private-sector marketing expenditures. It mandates independent audits for entities receiving over $50,000 annually and explicitly prohibits the use of program funds to promote the export of tobacco.

Furthermore, the Act establishes "graduation" requirements, phasing out and eventually terminating federal assistance after five years for both branded and generic promotion activities. The Secretary of Agriculture is granted limited authority to waive these participation caps in cases involving favorable trade rulings. The Act also defines small and medium-sized commercial entities based on employee counts (up to 50 employees and 51–500 employees, respectively) and requires the Secretary to issue implementing regulations within 60 days of enactment.
ref: Agricultural Market Promotion Program Amendments Act of 1993 - Amends the Agricultural Trade Act of 1978 with regard to the agricultural market promotion program to:  (1) give priority to, and obligate specified funds for, small and medium beginning exporters; (2) permit assistance for branded promotion only to supplement an entity's own promotional activities; (3) prohibit assistance for tobacco promotion; and (4) incrementally reduce and eliminate over a five-year period assistance for branded and generic promotion in a foreign country.

The DRAIN the SWAMP Act imposes stricter post-employment restrictions on executive branch political appointees to limit the influence of the "revolving door" between government service and lobbying. 

The bill amends title 18 of the United States Code to establish a five-year ban on former political appointees serving as registered lobbyists before the specific department or agency where they were previously employed. This restriction applies to individuals in Executive Schedule positions, noncareer Senior Executive Service roles, and Schedule C confidential or policy-determining positions. The Director of the Office of Government Ethics may grant waivers if the restrictions create undue staffing hardships and do not pose a risk of undue influence.

Additionally, the bill imposes a lifetime ban on former political appointees from registering as agents of foreign principals under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. These provisions apply to any political appointee whose government service ends on or after the bill's enactment date.
ref: Deter Revolving-door Appointments in our Nation; Stop Washington Appointees from becoming Manipulative Petitioners Act or the DRAIN the SWAMP Act This bill amends the federal criminal code to revise post-employment lobbying restrictions on senior executive branch officials and employees. Specifically, it imposes a five-year ban on communications by a former political appointee with the intent to influence officers or employees at their former executive branch agency or department.  The term political appointee includes certain senior political officials compensated on the Executive Schedule; limited term, limited emergency, and noncareer appointees in the Senior Executive Service; and employees in confidential or policy-determining positions in the excepted service. Additionally, the bill amends the Foreign Agents Registration Act of 1938 to impose a lifetime ban on lobbying by a former political appointee on behalf of a foreign government or foreign political party.

This bill regulates the use of Event Data Recorders (EDRs) in new automobiles. It mandates that dealers and manufacturers provide clear, written disclosure to consumers regarding the presence, location, and data-collection capabilities of EDRs, including their potential use in legal proceedings.

The bill establishes that vehicle owners maintain property rights over their EDRs and the data they record. Unauthorized retrieval of this data is prohibited, with limited exceptions for owner consent, court orders, vehicle repair or maintenance, and anonymized safety research. Furthermore, for vehicles model year 2009 or later, manufacturers must provide consumers with the option to enable or disable the EDR’s recording function.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is authorized to implement regulations for these disclosures and options within 180 days. Any violation of these requirements will be treated as an unfair or deceptive act under the Federal Trade Commission Act. The bill takes effect 180 days after its enactment.
ref:
Requires automobile dealers to disclose to each consumer at the time of purchase of a new automobile, and to include in the automobile's owner's manual, information on: (1) the presence and location of an event data recorder (EDR) in such automobile; and (2) the type of information recorded by the EDR, how such information is recorded, and the possible use of such information in law enforcement proceedings.

 Requires the EDR and any data recorded to be considered the property of the vehicle owner. Prohibits the retrieval of EDR data by anyone other than the vehicle owner, except : (1) with the owner's consent; (2) in response to a court order; (3) by a vehicle dealer or an automotive technician for servicing the vehicle; or (4) for improving vehicle safety, provided the identity of the registered owner or driver is not disclosed.

Prohibits persons from manufacturing automobiles for sale in the United States after 2008 (bearing a model year of 2009 or later) that are equipped with EDRs, unless those EDRs can be disabled by the consumer.

Treats a violation of EDR requirements of this Act as an unfair or deceptive act or practice under the Federal Trade Commission Act.

The "Stabilize Medicaid and CHIP Coverage Act" mandates 12-month continuous enrollment for individuals covered under Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP). 

Currently, many eligible enrollees lose health coverage due to administrative paperwork requirements, leading to disruptions in care, increased emergency room usage, and higher overall costs. By requiring that states ensure enrollees remain eligible and enrolled for a full 12-month period following an eligibility determination, the bill aims to improve access to primary care, enhance disease management, and reduce administrative burdens associated with frequent re-enrollment.

The legislation requires states to update their Medicaid and CHIP plans to reflect this continuous enrollment policy. The mandate generally takes effect 18 months after the date of enactment, though states have the option to implement the policy sooner. Provisions are included to allow for extensions in states where legislative action is required to amend the state plan.
ref: Stabilize Medicaid and CHIP Coverage Act - Amends title XIX (Medicaid) of the Social Security Act (SSA) to require a state Medicaid plan to provide 12-month continuous enrollment for an eligible individual, regardless of age.  Amends SSA title XXI (State Children's Health Insurance) (CHIP) to require a state CHIP plan also to provide 12-month continuous enrollment for an eligible individual.

The Agricultural Credit Equity Act of 1993 amends the Consolidated Farm and Rural Development Act to adjust federal agricultural lending standards. 

Key provisions include:
* **Loan Limits:** Guaranteed real estate and operating loan limits are indexed to local land values, allowing for higher loan caps in areas where land and building costs exceed the national average.
* **Hired Labor:** The Secretary of Agriculture may no longer deny loans solely because a farming operation employs more than two full-time workers. Loan eligibility will focus on the applicant’s active participation in farm activities and decision-making.
* **Loan Availability:** Requirements to assess the availability of credit elsewhere must now consider the actual availability of conventional funds for local agricultural producers.
* **Grower-Shipper Agreements:** The Act clarifies that federal loans are not prohibited for farmers who share sale proceeds with shippers of perishable commodities, provided the agreement is beneficial and necessary for marketing.
* **Emergency Loans:** The bill expands eligibility for emergency loans by allowing family members who collectively exceed family-farm size limits to qualify if their individual ownership interests meet the criteria.
ref:
Agricultural Credit Equity Act of 1993 - Amends the Consolidated Farm and Rural Development Act to provide for indexing of guaranteed agricultural real estate and operating loan limits in high cost areas. 
Eliminates maximum property limits in the down payment loan program. 
Prohibits the denial of agricultural real estate, operating, or emergency loans based upon:  (1) a farm's having more than two full-time employees; or (2) certain grower-shipper agreements.

The National Milestones to Measure Progress in Ending the Opioid Epidemic Act of 2018 directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services, in consultation with the DEA and the Office of National Drug Control Policy, to establish national indicators to track and curtail the opioid epidemic. Within 180 days of enactment, the Secretary must develop at least 10 metrics to measure success, aiming to significantly reverse opioid-related morbidity and mortality within five years. 

Required indicators include metrics on overdose rates, emergency room visits, provider education, recovery statistics, infection rates, treatment access, and harm reduction. The Secretary must set specific goals and annual targets for these indicators. If progress stalls, the Secretary may extend the five-year timeline, provided they offer a rationale and a revised strategy. Additionally, the Secretary must submit annual progress reports to Congress and the public. These reports must evaluate the effectiveness of federal programs, detail total federal investments, and provide annual status updates on reaching the established milestones.
ref: National Milestones to Measure Progress in Ending the Opioid Epidemic Act of 2018 This bill requires the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to develop national milestones to measure progress in reducing the opioid epidemic over a five-year period based on certain metrics, such as opioid-related overdoses, emergency room visits, and treatment admissions. HHS must submit annual reports and status updates, including evaluations of federal programs that are intended to address the opioid epidemic.

This bill designates a 40-mile segment of the Taunton River in Massachusetts as a component of the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System. The river is divided into four segments, alternating between "scenic" and "recreational" classifications.

The Secretary of the Interior is tasked with managing these segments in cooperation with the Taunton River Stewardship Council, utilizing the existing Taunton River Stewardship Plan (July 2005) to satisfy federal comprehensive management requirements. The legislation clarifies that the river will not be managed as a unit of the National Park System. 

Land acquisition by the Secretary is restricted to donations or owner-consented purchases, explicitly prohibiting the use of eminent domain (condemnation). Local zoning ordinances in the affected municipalities are deemed sufficient to meet federal standards. Additionally, the bill requires a report on energy resources within the designated area while stipulating that the designation does not affect state authority over hunting, fishing, and trapping, nor does it impact the supply of domestically produced energy.
ref:
Amends the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act (the Act) to designate specified segments of the Taunton River in Massachusetts as a component of the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System.

Requires the river segments to be managed in accordance with the Taunton River Stewardship Plan, dated July 2005, including any amendment to such Plan, that the Secretary of the Interior determines to be consistent with this Act.

Authorizes the Secretary, in order to provide for the protection, preservation, and enhancement of each river segment, to enter into cooperative agreements, which may include provisions for financial and other assistance, with: (1) the Commonwealth of Massachusetts (including the political subdivisions of Massachusetts); (2) the Taunton River Stewardship Council; and (3) any appropriate nonprofit, as determined by the Secretary.

Bars the river segments from being: (1) administered as a unit of the National Park System; or (2) subject to the laws (including regulations) that govern the administration of such System.

Considers the zoning ordinances adopted by specified towns and cities, including any provision of the zoning ordinances related to the conservation of floodplains, wetlands, and watercourses associated with any river segment designated by this Act, to satisfy each standard and requirement under the Act regarding the prohibition on the federal acquisition of certain lands by condemnation for inclusion in any national, wild, scenic, or recreational river area.

Authorizes the Secretary, respecting each river segment, to only acquire parcels of land by donation or with the owner's consent. Prohibits the acquisition of any parcel by condemnation.

Requires the Secretary, in consultation with the Secretary of Energy and private industry, to complete a report regarding the energy resources available on the lands and waters included in the segments of the Taunton River designated by this Act.

Prohibits anything in this Act from: (1) being construed as affecting the authority or responsibility of Massachusetts to manage or regulate fish and resident wildlife, including the authority to regulate hunting, fishing, trapping, and recreational shooting; (2) being construed as limiting access for hunting, fishing, trapping, or recreational shooting; or (3) impacting the supply of domestically-produced energy resources.
